sections.title: Understanding Level 2 Puzzles
sections.content: Level 2 puzzles are slightly more complex. Here, there may be 7–9 persons or objects, and the conclusion usually requires 3–4 steps instead of just 2. Often there are two variables (such as name + profession + color) or two dimensions (floor + flat). To solve them, it is useful to create two tables or one main table and one supporting table.

sections.title: Two-Variable Puzzles (Name + Profession + Color)
sections.content: Example: 7 people, 7 different professions, and 7 different shirt colors. First, list all the names. Then create separate columns for professions and colors. Fill in the direct information first. If it is stated that 'The Doctor does not wear a blue shirt', mark a cross between Doctor and Blue. Positive and negative conditions must be used together.

sections.title: Floor and Flat Puzzles
sections.content: There are 3 or 4 floors, and each floor has Flat 1 (West) and Flat 2 (East). Create a 2D table: rows for floors and columns for Flat 1 and Flat 2. If it is given that 'A lives on the third floor and is not in the West direction', place A in Flat 2 of the third floor. Pay attention to direction-related information.

sections.title: Complex Box Puzzles
sections.content: Seven to nine boxes are placed one above another. Determine the order from top to bottom. If it is stated that 'There are exactly three boxes between A and the red box, and A is not at the top', then two possibilities will arise. A may be positioned upward or downward relative to the red box. Create both cases separately and eliminate the one that violates any condition.

sections.title: Month and Date Puzzles
sections.content: There may be 3 or 4 months and two fixed dates (such as 5 and 18). Create a table with months in rows and dates (5 and 18) as columns. If it is stated that 'A is not on 18 in April', eliminate that position. When 3–4 positions are filled, the remaining positions are usually determined automatically.

sections.title: 3–4 Step Deduction Technique
sections.content: Step 1: Fill in direct information. Step 2: Use negative clues to eliminate options. Step 3: Apply comparison and distance-based conditions. Step 4: If two possibilities arise, create both cases and test them, eliminating the incorrect one.

sections.title: When to Create Parallel Cases
sections.content: If a condition gives two possible positions (such as 'exactly three boxes between them'), immediately create Case 1 and Case 2. Then verify with the remaining clues to see which case satisfies all conditions.

sections.title: Important Strategy
sections.content: 1. Always create a structured table. 2. Mark positive and negative conditions clearly. 3. Do not allow repetition of the same person or object. 4. Recheck after every step.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Misinterpreting directions (West/East). 2. Making assumptions without creating cases. 3. Ignoring negative conditions. 4. Getting confused by mixing two tables together.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 2 puzzles involve two or more variables. The solution typically takes 3–4 steps. Sometimes two cases must be created and one eliminated. Structured tables and systematic thinking are the key to solving them.

tricks.title: Double Table Trick
tricks.explanation: Create separate tables for Name vs Profession and Name vs Color.
tricks.example: Ravi is a Doctor but does not wear a red shirt — tick in Doctor column, cross in Red column.

tricks.title: West–East Memory Trick
tricks.explanation: Always assume Flat 1 as West and Flat 2 as East and keep it consistent.
tricks.example: Third floor: Flat 1 = West; Flat 2 = East.

tricks.title: Fixed Gap Rule
tricks.explanation: If there are 3 boxes between two boxes, the difference in their positions will be 4.
tricks.example: If A is at position 2, the other will be at position 6.

tricks.title: Above–Below Counting Shortcut
tricks.explanation: If there are 8 boxes in total and A is at position 4, then there are 3 above and 4 below.
tricks.example: Count positions quickly to check options.

tricks.title: Create Two Cases Immediately
tricks.explanation: If A can be on the third or fourth floor, create Case 1 and Case 2 and proceed.
tricks.example: Case 1: A on third floor; Case 2: A on fourth floor.

tricks.title: Fixed Columns in Date Puzzles
tricks.explanation: First create fixed columns for 5 and 18, then fill the months.

tricks.title: Conclusion from Elimination
tricks.explanation: If 5 out of 6 options are eliminated, the remaining one must be correct.
tricks.example: A can only be in IT — fill it directly.

tricks.title: Match the Last Two
tricks.explanation: When two positions and two persons remain, match conditions to determine the correct placement.
tricks.example: B is not on Monday, so C is Monday and B is Tuesday.

tricks.title: Cross-Marking Technique
tricks.explanation: Mark a cross on invalid combinations to avoid confusion.
tricks.example: Engineer ≠ Green, so mark X in that box.

tricks.title: Check After Every Step
tricks.explanation: After each new entry, verify it against all conditions.
tricks.example: Ensure no rule (like at least one per floor) is violated.
